problem: Zero-shot open-vocabulary object navigation handles only simple class queries (e.g. 'a toilet') and cannot handle natural-language queries with spatial relationships, such as 'the yellow ladder by the fire extinguisher'.
motivation: Real robots need to follow richer, relational language queries while still reusing a persistent open-vocabulary semantic map. Searching for such queries efficiently requires both grounding the relations and guiding exploration toward regions where the related objects co-occur.
key_idea: Decompose a spatially constrained query into simple object-level queries on semantic belief maps, intersect those maps to find regions where all objects co-exist, then validate candidates against the original query with an LVLM (DIV-Nav).
insight: Only the abstract is available, so no ablations can be cited. The abstract suggests that relaxing a relational query into per-object belief maps and deferring relation checking to an LVLM verification step keeps search efficient and real-time. It also suggests that frontier exploration objectives need to be adapted for spatial queries.
method: Decompose: an LLM splits complex natural-language instructions with spatial constraints and descriptive features into simpler object-level queries.
Semantic belief maps: each object-level query is scored on an online open-vocabulary semantic map, giving a per-object belief map.
Intersect: the individual belief maps are intersected to find regions of the mapped space where all queried objects co-exist.
Validate: candidate objects found in those regions are checked by an LVLM against the original spatially constrained command.
Frontier exploration adaptation: the frontier exploration objectives of online semantic mapping are modified to suit spatial-relation search queries.
